Why do a few supernovae cause gamma-ray bursts but most supernovae do not?

For a dying star to emit a gamma ray burst, there needs to be a few specific conditions which do not all coincide very frequently. First, the star must be extremely large, much larger than 25 solar masses and much larger than the stars that give you your average supernova upon death. Second, the star must be spinning extremely rapidly. Finally, the when the supernova(they're actually called hypernovas for stars this immense) occurs, it must not collapse into a more stable and extremely dense neutron star which are the results of most supernovas, it must form a black hole instead. Some supermassive stars can collapse into black holes without going supernova, a phenomenon which also emits gamma ray bursts. For these cases, the upper layers of the star rapidly collapse inwards during the formation of the black hole from the star's core. The turmoil in the magnetic field and the high rotation speed of the star serve to whip up the falling layers into a superheated spinning disk of plasma, which is then expelled at speeds exceeding ten percent the speed of light through the poles of the star, resulting in a devastating blast of every type of electromagnetic radiation, including gamma rays. With hypernovas, the process is very similar. If the star is spinning very quickly, the gases from the outer layers of the dying star are moving too quickly to be sucked into the emerging black hole and end up spinning around the black hole in a tight orbit, where they get superheated until they explode in an enormous, much more asymmetrical explosion.
